The Keeper of Harrow Point

Chapter 1

The lighthouse at Harrow Point had been automated for eleven years before the council remembered that it still had a keeper. His name was Oswin Pell, and he had not been paid since the spring of the year the lamp was converted. He lived in the lower rooms, ate from tins, and climbed the tower each evening to polish a lens that no longer needed polishing. When the letter from the council finally came, he read it standing at the foot of the stairs, folded it into quarters, and used it to prop up a table leg.

The harbour master drove out on the Thursday. He found Pell in the gallery with a cloth in his hand and the whole grey sea laid out below him. Neither of them mentioned the letter. They talked about the tide tables instead, which were wrong, and had been wrong for years.

Chapter 2

Pell kept a ledger of every ship that passed. He had begun it as a duty and continued it as a habit, and by now it ran to forty-one volumes in a hand that grew smaller each year. The entries were brief. A name, a time, a heading, and sometimes a single word about the weather. He had never been asked for the ledgers and did not expect to be.

In the autumn a surveyor arrived with instruments in a leather case. He wanted the volumes, he said, for a study of coastal traffic. Pell looked at him for a long moment and then went upstairs and brought down the first book, the one with the cracked spine, and laid it on the table between them like a thing that might still be alive.

Chapter 3

The surveyor stayed three weeks. He slept in the room that had been Pell's mother's and ate what Pell ate, and in the evenings he copied columns of figures by lamplight while the old man watched the water. They rarely spoke. On the last night the surveyor asked, without looking up, why the ledger had never once recorded Pell's own name.

Pell thought about it. Then he said that the book was for the ships, and he was only the one who saw them go by. In the morning the surveyor left with eleven volumes under his arm, and Pell climbed the tower as he always did and polished the lens until it shone.
